Espy
es-PY
verb
From the Old French espier, “to watch, to spy out,” of Germanic root and akin to our spy; hence to catch sight of, to descry at a distance, to search a thing out with the eye.

Biblical Definition

To espy is to catch sight of — to search out with the eye, whether by a startled glance or by a deliberate reconnaissance. Both senses are in Scripture. In Egypt, one of Joseph’s brethren opened his sack in the inn “and he espied his money; for, behold, it was in his sack’s mouth” (Gen 42:27) — a sudden sight that made their hearts fail them, for grace returned to guilty men looks at first like a trap. Jeremiah bids the inhabitant of Aroer “stand by the way, and espy” (Jer 48:19), to watch the road and ask the fugitives what is done: the watchman’s work, seeing the judgment before it arrives. Chiefly the word belongs to Caleb: “Forty years old was I when Moses the servant of the LORD sent me from Kadeshbarnea to espy out the land; and I brought him word again as it was in mine heart” (Jos 14:7). Twelve men espied the same hills, the same walled cities, the same giants; ten brought back an evil report and one brought back God. The eye reports what the heart believes. But the word’s deepest use is not of man at all. Ezekiel says the LORD brought Israel “into a land that I had espied for them, flowing with milk and honey, which is the glory of all lands” (Eze 20:6). Before ever a spy crossed the border, God had surveyed the inheritance and chosen it for His people.

Webster 1828 Definition

To catch sight of; to descry; to search out or discover with the eye.

expand to see more

ESPY, to see at a distance; to descry; to discover by the eye.

From Old French espier, “to watch, to spy out”; akin to spy.

It denotes both a sudden catching of sight and a deliberate searching out.

Moses sent Caleb to espy out the land of Canaan (Jos 14:7).

The LORD Himself espied the land for His people beforehand (Eze 20:6).

Key Scripture

Gen 42:27 — "And as one of them opened his sack to give his ass provender in the inn, he espied his money; for, behold, it was in his sack's mouth."

Jos 14:7 — "Forty years old was I when Moses the servant of the LORD sent me from Kadeshbarnea to espy out the land; and I brought him word again as it was in mine heart."

Jer 48:19 — "O inhabitant of Aroer, stand by the way, and espy; ask him that fleeth, and her that escapeth, and say, What is done?"

Eze 20:6 — "In the day that I lifted up mine hand unto them, to bring them forth of the land of Egypt into a land that I had espied for them, flowing with milk and honey, which is the glory of all lands:"

Modern Corruption

Not a contested doctrine but a plain word for catching sight; it recovers that the eye reports what the heart believes, and that God espied the inheritance first.

expand to see more

The word rebukes the conceit that seeing is believing. Twelve men were sent to espy out Canaan, and twelve men saw the same land — the same clusters of Eshcol, the same walled cities, the same sons of Anak. Ten espied and said, We be not able; Caleb espied and brought word again as it was in his heart, We are well able to overcome it. The difference was not in the eye but in the heart behind the eye. Unbelief looks at giants and forgets God; faith looks at giants and remembers Him. Every man reports the land he was sent to see, but he reports it in the accent of what he believes about the LORD who sent him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God espied first. Ezekiel says the LORD brought His people into a land that He had espied for them, flowing with milk and honey, the glory of all lands — surveyed, chosen, and appointed before ever a spy set foot in it. The searching out of the twelve did not discover the inheritance; it only confirmed what God had already seen and given. So it is with every mercy: we come at last to espy what sovereign love long ago prepared, and the brethren who trembled at the money in the sack’s mouth found it was not a snare but a gift.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means to catch sight of, to descry, to search out with the eye.

expand to see more

Espy — Old French espier, “to watch, to spy out.”

Of Germanic root, and akin to the English spy.

It denotes catching sight of a thing, or searching it out deliberately.

Caleb was sent to espy out the land and brought word again in faith (Jos 14:7).

The LORD espied the land for His people before they saw it (Eze 20:6).

Usage

"He espied his money in the sack’s mouth: returning mercy first looked like a snare."

"Twelve espied one land; the eye reported what the heart believed about God."

"The LORD espied the inheritance for His people before ever a spy crossed the border."
